report:
## Conclusion: The answer is **yes** — CT screening does reduce lung cancer mortality in heavy smokers

Your initial belief that the answer is "no" is not supported by the evidence. Two landmark randomized controlled trials and subsequent meta-analyses demonstrate a clear mortality benefit.

### Key Evidence

**The NLST Trial (2011):** The National Lung Screening Trial enrolled 53,454 high-risk current and former heavy smokers. It found a **20% relative reduction** in lung cancer mortality with low-dose CT screening compared to chest radiography (247 vs. 309 deaths per 100,000 person-years; P=0.004). It also showed a 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873))

**The NELSON Trial (2020):** This European RCT confirmed the NLST findings, showing that volume-based low-dose CT screening produced **substantially lower lung cancer mortality** than no screening among high-risk persons, with an overdiagnosis rate of only ~10%. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793))

**Meta-analyses & Guidelines:** A 2022 *Lancet* review concluded that RCTs including NLST and NELSON "have shown reduced mortality with lung cancer screening with low-dose CT." The NCI and CDC both recommend LDCT screening for high-risk heavy smokers based on this evidence. ([The Lancet](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(22)01694-4/fulltext), [NCI PDQ](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/hp/lung-screening-pdq))

### Important Caveats

- **Smaller trials (DANTE, ITALUNG)** individually lacked statistical power to show significance, but pooled analyses still showed a 15% mortality reduction in men. ([AJRCCM](https://academic.oup.com/ajrccm/article/192/3/398/8504781))
- **Harms exist:** false-positive rates (~20–25%), unnecessary invasive procedures, radiation exposure, and overdiagnosis are real concerns that temper but do not negate the benefit. ([JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2777242))

In summary, the evidence consistently supports that regular low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer death in heavy current and former smokers by approximately 20–26%.
